This section introduces the discovery and study of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and explains why it is important for understanding the universe. It also describes the Planck mission and its goals, focusing on measuring the CMB to test the standard cosmological model.

TERMS:
- cosmic microwave background (CMB) — radiation left over from the early universe
- hot big bang cosmology — theory describing the universe's expansion from a hot, dense state
- anisotropies — small differences or variations
- fluctuations — small changes or irregularities
- primordial — existing from the beginning
- scale-invariant — properties that remain the same at different scales
- inflationary cosmology — theory explaining the rapid expansion of the universe shortly after the Big Bang
- angular power spectrum — a way to describe the distribution of temperature variations in the CMB
- Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) — satellite used to measure the CMB
- micro-Kelvin — extremely small temperature measurements
- Galactic emission — light and radiation from the Milky Way galaxy
- polarization anisotropies — variations in the direction of the CMB's electromagnetic waves
- micro-lensing — a gravitational effect that can bend and magnify light
- BOOMERang — balloon-based experiment that measured CMB anisotropies
- MAXIMA — balloon-based experiment that measured CMB anisotropies
- standard (base) ΛCDM model — a simple model describing the universe's composition and evolution
- large-angle "anomalies" — unexpected features in the CMB
- non-Gaussianity — statistical properties of the CMB that deviate from a Gaussian distribution
- isocurvature modes — a type of primordial fluctuation
- topological defects — irregularities in the fabric of space and time
